units.title: Hello, Crystal
units.summary: Write your first Crystal programs: print text and numbers with puts, print and p, and let Crystal calculate.

lesson.md: Crystal is a programming language that is easy to read and runs fast. A Crystal program is a list of instructions. The computer runs them from top to bottom, one line after the other. Your first instruction is `puts`: it prints a value and then starts a new line.

lesson.code: puts "Hello, Crystal!"

lesson.md: Text in double quotes is called a **string**. Every `puts` prints its own line. In Crystal, strings always use double quotes, like `"Hi"`. Single quotes are only for one single character, like `'A'`.

lesson.code:
puts "Hello"
puts "World"
puts "Crystal is fast"

lesson.md: Numbers need no quotes. Crystal calculates with `+` (plus), `-` (minus), `*` (times) and `/` (divided by). Whole numbers are called **integers**. The result of `/` is always a number with a decimal point, a **float**: `7 / 2` is `3.5` and `6 / 2` is `3.0`. Use `//` to divide and drop the part after the decimal point: `7 // 2` is `3`. `%` gives the remainder of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`.

lesson.code:
puts 2 + 3
puts 10 - 4
puts 3 * 4
puts 7 / 2
puts 6 / 2
puts 7 // 2
puts 7 % 2

lesson.md: Quotes make a big difference. `"2"` with quotes is text, `2` without quotes is a number. `+` between two strings joins them, and `+` between two numbers adds them.

lesson.code:
puts "2" + "3"
puts 2 + 3

lesson.md: Crystal checks your whole program before it runs it. This step is called **compiling**. `puts "Age: " + 30` does not compile, because `+` cannot join a string and a number. You see an error message, and no line of the program runs. You learn how to put numbers into text in the Strings unit.

`print` prints a value **without** a new line at the end, so the next output continues on the same line. `p` prints a value the way Crystal sees it: a string keeps its quotes. Programmers use `p` to check values while they work.

lesson.code:
print "Hello, "
print "World"
puts "!"
p "Crystal"
p 42

lesson.md: Everything after a `#` on a line is a **comment**. Crystal ignores it. In this course, comments only show results, for example `puts 2 + 3 # 5`.

card: `puts "Hi"` prints and starts a new line
`p "Hi"` shows the value with its quotes: `"Hi"`

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables, let Crystal find their types, and convert between Int32, Float64 and String.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. `=` stores the value on the right under the name on the left. After that, you can use the name instead of the value.

lesson.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
puts name
puts age

lesson.md: You can give a variable a new value at any time. The new value can use the old one. `score += 5` is a short way to write `score = score + 5`. `-=` and `*=` work the same way.

lesson.code:
score = 10
score = score + 5
puts score
score += 1
puts score
score *= 2
puts score

lesson.md: Crystal knows the **type** of every value before the program runs. You do not have to write the type: the compiler finds it from the value. This is called **type inference**. `typeof(x)` shows the type of `x`. Whole numbers are `Int32`, numbers with a decimal point are `Float64`, text is `String`, and `true` and `false` are `Bool`.

lesson.code:
age = 36
price = 4.5
name = "Ada"
ready = true
puts typeof(age)
puts typeof(price)
puts typeof(name)
puts typeof(ready)

lesson.md: The `32` in `Int32` means that the number uses 32 bits of memory. An `Int32` holds whole numbers up to about 2 billion. For bigger numbers, use `Int64`: write `_i64` after the number. You can put `_` between digits to make long numbers easier to read.

lesson.code:
big = 3_000_000_000_i64
puts big
puts typeof(big)
puts 1_000_000

lesson.md: You can also write the type yourself: `count : Int32 = 5`. Then `count` can only hold an `Int32`. If you later write `count = "eight"`, the program does not compile.

lesson.code:
count : Int32 = 5
count = 8
puts count

lesson.md: Methods convert values to other types. `to_i` makes an integer, `to_f` makes a float, and `to_s` makes a string. `3.9.to_i` is `3`: it drops the part after the decimal point.

lesson.code:
puts "42".to_i + 1
puts 3.9.to_i
puts 5.to_f
puts 7.to_s + "0"

lesson.md: A name that starts with an uppercase letter is a **constant**, for example `MAX = 100`. You cannot give a constant a new value. Names are case sensitive: `price` and `Price` are two different names.

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Put values into text with #{}, and work with strings: size, upcase, includes? and single characters.

lesson.md: **Interpolation** puts values into a string. Inside double quotes, write `#{` and `}` around a variable or a calculation. Crystal replaces it with the value, also when the value is a number. Here `#` does not start a comment.

lesson.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
puts "#{name} is #{age} years old."
puts "Next year: #{age + 1}"
lesson.output:
Ada is 36 years old.
Next year: 37

lesson.md: Strings have **methods**. You call a method with a dot after the value. `size` gives the number of characters. `upcase` and `downcase` change letters to uppercase or lowercase, `capitalize` makes only the first letter uppercase, and `reverse` turns the string around.

lesson.code:
word = "crystal"
puts word.size
puts word.upcase
puts word.capitalize
puts word.reverse

lesson.md: A method whose name ends with `?` answers a question with `true` or `false`. `includes?` checks if a text contains another text. `starts_with?` and `ends_with?` check the start and the end. `empty?` checks if a string has no characters.

lesson.code:
text = "I like Crystal"
puts text.includes?("like")
puts text.starts_with?("You")
puts text.ends_with?("al")
puts "".empty?

lesson.md: `[]` with a number, the **index**, gets one character. Counting starts at `0`, so `word[0]` is the first character. `-1` is the last one. A single character has the type `Char` and is written in single quotes, like `'C'`.

lesson.code:
word = "Crystal"
p word[0]
p word[-1]
puts typeof(word[0])

lesson.md: `+` joins two strings, and `*` repeats a string. `strip` removes spaces at the start and at the end. You can call several methods one after the other: Crystal runs them from left to right.

lesson.code:
puts "ab" + "cd"
puts "-" * 5
puts "  hi  ".strip.upcase

lesson.md: Uppercase and lowercase letters are different characters. `"Crystal".includes?("crystal")` is `false`. Call `downcase` first if case should not matter.

card: `"Hi #{name}"` puts a value into a string

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program decide with if, elsif, else, unless, case and the ternary operator, and handle nil safely.

lesson.md: A comparison gives a `Bool`. `==` checks if two values are equal, `!=` checks if they are different. `<` means less than, `>` greater than, `<=` less than or equal, `>=` greater than or equal. Be careful: `=` stores a value, `==` compares.

lesson.code:
age = 20
puts age >= 18
puts age == 21
puts age != 21

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The lines between `if` and `end` are the **body**; indent them by two spaces. The body after `else` runs when the condition is `false`.

lesson.code:
temp = 25
if temp > 20
  puts "Warm"
else
  puts "Cold"
end

lesson.md: `elsif` checks another condition. Crystal checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first body whose condition is `true`.

lesson.code:
score = 75
if score >= 90
  puts "A"
elsif score >= 70
  puts "B"
else
  puts "C"
end

lesson.md: `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are true. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is true. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and back. `unless` is the opposite of `if`: its body runs when the condition is `false`. For one line, you can write `if` or `unless` at the end of the line.

lesson.code:
age = 15
member = true
puts "Welcome" if age >= 12 && member
unless age >= 18
  puts "Too young for the late show"
end
lesson.output:
Welcome
Too young for the late show

lesson.md: `case` compares one value with several `when` branches. A `when` can list several values, separated by commas, or a **range** like `1..5`, which means all numbers from 1 to 5. `else` runs when no `when` matches.

lesson.code:
day = 6
case day
when 6, 7
  puts "Weekend"
when 1..5
  puts "Workday"
else
  puts "Unknown day"
end

lesson.md: The **ternary operator** is a short `if` with `else` in one line: `condition ? a : b`. It gives `a` when the condition is `true` and `b` when it is `false`.

lesson.code:
n = 7
puts n % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd"

lesson.md: Sometimes there is no value. Crystal uses `nil` for this. `"crystal".index('s')` gives the position of the first `s`, or `nil` if there is none. `if pos` runs its body only when `pos` is not `nil`, and inside the body Crystal knows that `pos` is a number. `nil?` checks if a value is `nil`. The compiler does not let you calculate with a value that might be `nil`, so you cannot forget this check.

lesson.code:
pos = "crystal".index('s')
if pos
  puts "Found at #{pos}"
else
  puts "Not found"
end
puts "crystal".index('z').nil?

card: `&&` and, `||` or, `!` not, `unless` means if not

units.title: Loops and ranges
units.summary: Repeat code with times, each and while, count with ranges, and control loops with break and next.

lesson.md: Programs often repeat things. `3.times` runs code three times. The code between `do` and `end` is a **block**: a piece of code that you give to a method.

lesson.code:
3.times do
  puts "Hi"
end

lesson.md: A block can take a **parameter**, a name between two `|` bars. `times` passes the number of the round to the block. It starts counting at `0`.

lesson.code:
3.times do |i|
  puts "Round #{i}"
end

lesson.md: A **range** is a sequence of numbers. `1..3` contains 1, 2 and 3. With three dots, `1...3` stops before the end and contains only 1 and 2. `each` runs the block once for every number. For a short block, you can write `{` and `}` instead of `do` and `end`.

lesson.code:
(1..3).each do |n|
  puts n * 10
end
(1...3).each { |n| puts n }

lesson.md: Ranges have useful methods. `sum` adds up all numbers, and `includes?` checks if a number is in the range.

lesson.code:
total = (1..4).sum
puts total
puts (1..10).includes?(7)

lesson.md: `while` repeats its body as long as the condition is `true`. Change a variable in the body so that the condition becomes `false` at some point. Otherwise the loop never ends.

lesson.code:
n = 1
while n < 50
  n *= 3
end
puts n

lesson.md: `break` leaves a loop at once. `next` skips the rest of the body and goes on with the next round. `odd?` and `even?` check if a number is odd or even.

lesson.code:
(1..10).each do |n|
  next if n.odd?
  break if n > 6
  puts n
end

card: `while x < 10` … `end` repeats while the condition is true
`break` leaves the loop, `next` skips to the next round

units.title: Methods
units.summary: Write your own methods with def, restrict argument types, return values, and use default and named arguments.

lesson.md: A **method** is a piece of code with a name. You define it once with `def` and the name, and end it with `end`. After that, you run it by writing its name. This is called **calling** the method.

lesson.code:
def greet
  puts "Hello!"
end

greet
greet

lesson.md: A method can take **parameters** in parentheses. `name : String` is a **type restriction**: the method only accepts a `String` for `name`. When you call the method, the values in parentheses are the **arguments**.

lesson.code:
def greet(name : String)
  puts "Hello, #{name}!"
end

greet("Ada")
greet("Bob")

lesson.md: A method gives back a **return value**: the value of its last line. You can write the type of the return value after the parentheses, like `: Int32`. Then the compiler checks that the method really returns an `Int32`.

lesson.code:
def square(n : Int32) : Int32
  n * n
end

puts square(4)
puts square(3) + 1

lesson.md: `return` leaves the method at once and gives back the value after it. This is useful to handle a special case first.

lesson.code:
def sign(n : Int32) : String
  return "zero" if n == 0
  n > 0 ? "positive" : "negative"
end

puts sign(5)
puts sign(0)
puts sign(-2)

lesson.md: A parameter can have a **default value**: `name = "World"`. When you call the method without this argument, the default value is used. You can also write the parameter names in a call, like `area(height: 2, width: 5)`. With **named arguments**, the order does not matter.

lesson.code:
def greet(name = "World")
  puts "Hello, #{name}!"
end

def area(width : Int32, height : Int32)
  width * height
end

greet
greet("Kim")
puts area(height: 2, width: 5)

lesson.md: In Crystal, a method whose name ends with `?` returns `true` or `false`, like `even?`. You can write such methods yourself.

lesson.code:
def adult?(age : Int32) : Bool
  age >= 18
end

puts adult?(20)
puts adult?(12)

lesson.md: Type restrictions protect you. `square("4")` does not compile, because `"4"` is a `String` and `square` needs an `Int32`. The compiler finds this mistake before the program runs.

card: `def name(x : Int32) : Int32` … `end` defines a method
The last line is the return value; `return` leaves early

units.title: Arrays and hashes
units.summary: Keep many values in arrays and hashes, and work with them using each, map, select and sum.

lesson.md: An **array** is an ordered list of values. Write the values between `[` and `]`, separated by commas. `[]` with an index gets one item: counting starts at `0`, and `-1` is the last item. `size` gives the number of items.

lesson.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
puts fruits[0]
puts fruits[-1]
puts fruits.size
p fruits

lesson.md: `<<` adds an item at the end. All items of an array have the same type: `[1, 2, 3]` is an `Array(Int32)`. An empty array has no items to show its type, so you write it yourself: `[] of String`.

lesson.code:
names = [] of String
names << "Ada"
names << "Bob"
p names
puts typeof([1, 2, 3])

lesson.md: `each` runs a block once for every item. The block parameter holds the current item.

lesson.code:
prices = [3, 5, 2]
prices.each do |price|
  puts "Price: #{price}"
end

lesson.md: `map` makes a new array with the result of the block for every item. `select` keeps only the items for which the block is `true`. `sum` adds up all items, and `includes?` checks if an item is in the array. `&.even?` is a short way to write the block `{ |n| n.even? }`.

lesson.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
p nums.map { |n| n * 10 }
p nums.select(&.even?)
puts nums.sum
puts nums.includes?(3)

lesson.md: `nums[10]` stops the program with an error when the array has no item at index 10. Add a `?` to get `nil` instead: `nums[10]?`.

A **hash** stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**. Write them between `{` and `}` with `=>` between key and value. `ages["Ada"]` reads the value for the key `"Ada"`, and `ages["Cy"] = 41` adds or changes a pair. `ages["Dan"]?` gives `nil` when the key is missing, and `has_key?` checks if a key exists.

lesson.code:
ages = {"Ada" => 36, "Bob" => 25}
puts ages["Ada"]
ages["Cy"] = 41
puts ages.size
p ages["Dan"]?
puts ages.has_key?("Bob")

lesson.md: `each` on a hash passes two values to the block: the key and the value.

lesson.code:
stock = {"apple" => 3, "pear" => 0}
stock.each do |fruit, count|
  puts "#{fruit}: #{count}"
end

units.title: Classes and structs
units.summary: Build your own types with class and struct, store data in instance variables, and use getter and property.

lesson.md: A **class** is a plan for **objects**. An object keeps data together with the methods that work on it. Class names start with an uppercase letter. `Dog.new("Rex")` creates a new object, and Crystal calls the method `initialize` with the arguments.

lesson.code:
class Dog
  def initialize(name : String)
    @name = name
  end

  def bark
    puts "#{@name} says woof"
  end
end

rex = Dog.new("Rex")
rex.bark

lesson.md: `@name` is an **instance variable**. Every object has its own copy, and all methods of the object can use it. The short form `def initialize(@name : String)` stores the argument in `@name` directly.

lesson.code:
class Dog
  def initialize(@name : String)
  end

  def bark
    puts "#{@name} says woof"
  end
end

Dog.new("Rex").bark
Dog.new("Bella").bark
lesson.output:
Rex says woof
Bella says woof

lesson.md: Code outside the class cannot read instance variables. `getter name : String` creates a method `name` that reads `@name`. `property score : Int32` creates a method to read `@score` and one to change it.

lesson.code:
class Player
  getter name : String
  property score : Int32

  def initialize(@name : String)
    @score = 0
  end
end

player = Player.new("Ada")
player.score = 10
player.score += 5
puts "#{player.name}: #{player.score}"

lesson.md: A `getter` can only read. `player.name = "Bob"` does not compile, because there is no method to change `name`. Use `property` when code outside the class should change a value.
Methods can change instance variables. `getter count = 0` creates `@count` with the start value `0` and a method to read it.

lesson.code:
class Counter
  getter count = 0

  def increment
    @count += 1
  end
end

counter = Counter.new
3.times { counter.increment }
puts counter.count

lesson.md: A **struct** looks like a class, but it is **copied** when you store it in another variable. Objects of a class are **shared**: two variables can point to the same object. In this program, changing `b` does not change the struct `a`, but changing `y` also changes the object `x`.

lesson.code:
struct Point
  property x : Int32

  def initialize(@x : Int32)
  end
end

class Bag
  property x : Int32

  def initialize(@x : Int32)
  end
end

a = Point.new(1)
b = a
b.x = 9
puts a.x

x = Bag.new(1)
y = x
y.x = 9
puts x.x

lesson.md: Use a struct for small values like a point or a color. Use a class for things that change over time, like a player or a shopping cart.

card: `getter name : String` reads, `property score : Int32` reads and writes
